findings.issue: The certificate chain is verified only when BOTH `VerifyCertificateChain` (default true) AND `OrgSigningPublicKey` are set: `if (options.VerifyCertificateChain && options.OrgSigningPublicKey is { } orgKey)`. A caller that constructs `new ContainerOpenOptions { ExpectedKind = ... }` and forgets the org key gets a reader that silently accepts ANY container: the signature is checked against the Ed25519 key carried inside the manifest's own producer certificate, so an attacker generates an identity, self-issues a DeviceCertificateBody, signs the container with it and passes every check. Revocation is skipped too (revocation is only evaluated inside CertificateChain.Verify). The spec requires the reader to verify the certificate chain before decrypting; making that depend on a nullable field that defaults to null turns the secure path into the opt-in path. No test covers the null-org-key case (ContainerWorld.Options always supplies it).
findings.fix: In ContainerReader.Open, after deserializing the manifest: `if (options.VerifyCertificateChain) { if (options.OrgSigningPublicKey is not { Length: DeviceIdentity.PublicKeySize } orgKey) throw new CryptoException(ErrorCode.BadSignature, "The organisation key is required to check who produced this file."); CertificateChain.Verify(manifest.Producer, orgKey, options.Revocations, now, options.IssuerCertificate); }` so that skipping the chain requires the caller to write `VerifyCertificateChain = false` explicitly. Add a test asserting that opening a container produced by a self-issued certificate fails, and a test that an options object without OrgSigningPublicKey throws instead of accepting.

findings.issue: Path-escape in ExtractTo. `var target = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(root, expected.Name)); if (!target.StartsWith(root, StringComparison.Ordinal))` is a string-prefix test against a root that has no trailing separator. Verified by probe: root `C:\tmp\out`, entry name `..\outside\evil.txt` resolves to `C:\tmp\outside\evil.txt`, and `StartsWith("C:\tmp\out")` is true, so the file is written outside the chosen folder. Entry names come from the manifest of a foreign producer and are never validated on the read side (ContainerEntrySource validates only on the write side), and the comparison is also case-sensitive on a case-insensitive file system.
findings.fix: Build the comparison root with a trailing separator and compare case-insensitively on Windows: `var rootWithSep = root.EndsWith(Path.DirectorySeparatorChar) ? root : root + Path.DirectorySeparatorChar; if (!target.StartsWith(rootWithSep, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) throw ...` (or use `Path.GetRelativePath(root, target)` and reject a result that is rooted or starts with ".."). Additionally validate every `expected.Name` right after the manifest is parsed with the same rules ContainerEntrySource applies on write (no '\\', not rooted, no ".." segment), and add a test that a container whose manifest names `..\\outside\\evil.txt` is refused.

findings.issue: Malformed untrusted input escapes as exception types outside the CryptoException contract. Verified by probe against the built assembly: (a) `CanonicalJson.Deserialize<RevocationEntry>("{\"deviceId\":\"d\",\"revokedAt\":\"not-a-date\"}")` throws FormatException — UtcInstantConverter.Read calls DateTimeOffset.Parse, and System.Text.Json only wraps JsonException, so the catch in Deserialize never sees it; (b) `Deserialize<ContainerManifest>` of `{"type":"sync","version":1,"mode":"officeKey","createdAt":"...","producer":{"signature":"AA"},"entries":[]}` returns a manifest whose `Producer` is non-null but whose `Producer.Body` is null, and ContainerReader.Open passes its `manifest.Producer is null` guard and then dereferences `manifest.Producer.Body.Ed25519Pub` → NullReferenceException. Both are reachable from a hostile `.wakeel-*` file before any signature check, so the UI error mapper sees an unmapped exception instead of ErrorCode.Corrupt.
findings.fix: In UtcInstantConverter.Read use `DateTimeOffset.TryParse(text, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.AssumeUniversal | DateTimeStyles.AdjustToUniversal, out var value)` and `throw new JsonException(...)` when it fails. In ContainerReader.Open, immediately after deserialization, validate the shape before using it: Producer, Producer.Body, Producer.Signature, Entries and every entry's Name/Sha256 non-null, throwing CryptoException(ErrorCode.Corrupt). Do the same in DeviceCertificate/RevocationList/PairingRequest/PairingAccept verify helpers (a null Body currently serialises to the 4-byte literal "null"). Add tests feeding each of these malformed documents and asserting CryptoException with ErrorCode.Corrupt.

findings.issue: PairingAccept.Issue performs no verification of the request it answers: it issues a phone device certificate over `request.Body.Ed25519Pub`/`X25519Pub` and seals BOTH the session key and the office key to `request.Body.X25519Pub` without ever calling VerifySignature/VerifyToken/EnsureAcceptable. Since pairing requests arrive as a file dropped in the phone's shared folder (ARCHITECTURE §7), any process that can write that folder obtains the office key sealed to its own key if the caller in B1/B7 forgets the separate EnsureAcceptable call. It also copies OrgId and OfficeId from the attacker-controlled request instead of from the PC certificate, so an unverified request can mint a certificate naming another office.
findings.fix: Change the signature to `Issue(PairingRequest request, PairingQrPayload invitation, DeviceCertificate pcCertificate, ...)` and call `request.EnsureAcceptable(invitation, timeProvider);` as the first statement, so verification cannot be skipped. Build the certificate body from `pcCertificate.Body.OrgId` and `pcCertificate.Body.OfficeId` (the request's values have already been compared to the invitation by EnsureAcceptable). Add a test that Issue throws for a request whose token proof or self-signature is wrong.

findings.issue: BuildPayload stages the complete PLAINTEXT of the container (for `.wakeel-backup` the whole database and vault; for `.wakeel-setup` the OfficeKey, the device seeds and the certificate) in `Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "wakeel-" + Path.GetRandomFileName())` opened with plain FileMode.Create/FileAccess.Write and removed only by a best-effort File.Delete in the finally block. A crash, a power cut or a swallowed IOException leaves the unencrypted secrets in the user's %TEMP% folder, outside the protected ProgramData tree, and delete is not a wipe. ContainerReader.DecryptPayload does the same for the decrypt direction but at least uses FileOptions.DeleteOnClose.
findings.fix: Open the staging file once as `new FileStream(temporary, FileMode.CreateNew, FileAccess.ReadWrite, FileShare.None, 81920, FileOptions.DeleteOnClose)`, hand that single stream to BuildPayload (leaveOpen on the inner ZipArchive), then `Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` and encrypt straight from it instead of reopening by path; the handle guarantees removal even on an abnormal exit. Also add a `string? StagingDirectory` to ContainerWriteRequest (and the matching option on ContainerOpenOptions) so the Desktop host can point staging at C:\ProgramData\Wakeel rather than %TEMP%.

findings.issue: The container format cannot express the administrator's recovery copy that AGREEMENT item 17 and ARCHITECTURE §3/§4 require ("مدير النظام يستطيع فتح أي نسخة أو نسخة احتياطية أو مراسلة"; the §4 table lists `.wakeel-backup` as "password + AdminWrap"). PayloadMode is single-valued and `SealedKey` is populated only in SealedFor mode, so a password-protected backup or a message sealed to one recipient can never be opened by the organisation key. Putting installation.key (which does carry an AdminWrap) inside the payload does not help, because payload.bin itself is locked by the password. The manifest is signed and versioned, so this must be settled before the first file ships.
findings.fix: Add an optional `string? AdminSealedKey` to ContainerManifest, filled by the writer for every kind whose §4 row requires it with `Base64Url.Encode(DeviceIdentity.SealFor(orgAgreementPublicKey, contentKey, "wakeel.container.adminkey"))`, plus `ContainerKeySource.ForAdmin(DeviceIdentity orgIdentity)` on the read side that recovers the content key from that field (and an `OrgAgreementPublicKey` on ContainerWriteRequest). Keep manifest Version at 1 by landing it now, and test that the org identity opens a password-mode backup and a sealedFor message without the password/recipient key.

findings.issue: The phone cannot complete the org→pc→phone chain from the pairing exchange. PairingAcceptBody carries PcDeviceId but not the PC certificate, and the QR payload carries only pcX25519Pub, not the PC's Ed25519 key — so on the phone side `accept.VerifySignature(pcSigningPublicKey)` has no key to use and `CertificateChain.Verify(phoneCert, orgPub, ..., issuerCertificate)` has no issuer certificate to pass. The test that exercises this (The_whole_pairing_exchange...) uses the in-process `pki.PcCertificate`, which the real phone never receives.
findings.fix: Add `DeviceCertificate PcCertificate` to PairingAcceptBody (issued by the org, already held by the computer) so the phone can verify accept signature → PC certificate → org root → phone certificate, and assert inside a new phone-side test that verification uses only material that actually crosses the cable (QR payload + accept file + org key from the setup file).

findings.issue: The 5-byte stream header `[version:1][chunkSize:4]` written by EncryptStream is not authenticated: BuildFrameAssociatedData binds the constant FormatVersion, the caller AD, the frame index and the final flag, but not the declared chunk size. An attacker can rewrite chunkSize in payload.bin (inside a container this is caught by the signature, but the primitive is public API), turning a valid stream into 'invalid frame length' or forcing a 16 MB buffer allocation. Integrity of the data itself is unaffected.
findings.fix: Keep the 5-byte header in a local and pass it into BuildFrameAssociatedData so every frame authenticates `header || callerAd || index || finalFlag`; the decrypt side reads the header first and uses the same bytes.

findings.issue: ContainerWriter.SigningInput signs a bare 64-byte `sha256(manifest) || sha256(payload)` with no domain separator, while the same Ed25519 device key also signs certificate bodies, revocation lists, pairing requests and pairing accepts. There is no practical attack today (the other structures are canonical JSON starting with '{'), but cross-protocol separation is cheap and belongs in the format before it ships.
findings.fix: Prefix a constant label: sign `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("wakeel.container.sig|v1") || manifestHash || payloadHash`, and give each signed JSON body its own label the same way (e.g. "wakeel.cert|v1" prepended to the canonical bytes).

findings.issue: KeyWrap carries the salt twice: FromSecret stores `(byte[])kdf.Salt.Clone()` in the `Salt` field while OpenWithSecret derives exclusively from `wrap.Kdf`. The `Salt` field is dead weight that can silently disagree with the salt that actually opens the wrap, and it is serialised into installation.key, inviting a future reader to use the wrong one.
findings.fix: Either drop the `Salt` member from the record (the spec's field list is satisfied by Kdf.Salt) or, if the field must stay for the serialised shape, assert in Expect() that `wrap.Kdf is null || wrap.Salt.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(wrap.Kdf.Salt)` and throw CryptoException(ErrorCode.Corrupt) otherwise.

findings.issue: Write(string path, ...) opens the destination with FileMode.Create and writes in place, so an interrupted or failing export leaves a truncated `.wakeel-*` file in packages\outbox or the backups folder, where the user cannot tell it from a good one. InstallationKeyFile already does temp+rename; containers do not.
findings.fix: Write to `path + ".tmp"` and `File.Move(temp, path, overwrite: true)` on success, deleting the temp in a catch/finally — the same pattern as InstallationKeyFile.Save.

findings.issue: Three small verification gaps: (1) the revocation list's `Body.OrgId` is never compared with the certificate's OrgId, so a list signed by the org for a different organisation is accepted as authoritative; (2) the list's IssuedAt is never inspected, so an old list is indistinguishable from a current one; (3) when a phone certificate is checked, `maxAge` is propagated to the recursive VerifyNode call for the issuing PC certificate, so a caller who passes a freshness window for the leaf also rejects a perfectly valid but older PC certificate.
findings.fix: Compare `revocations.Body.OrgId` with `certificate.Body.OrgId` (ordinal) and throw BadSignature on a mismatch; expose an optional `maxRevocationListAge` so a stale list can be reported; and pass `maxAge: null` in the recursive VerifyNode call for the issuer, keeping the freshness window on the presented leaf only.

findings.issue: ReadEntry(name, key) is implemented as ReadEntries(key) plus a dictionary lookup, so reading one small entry out of a multi-gigabyte `.wakeel-backup` decrypts the whole payload and buffers every entry in memory. ExtractTo streams correctly, ReadEntry does not.
findings.fix: Implement ReadEntry directly: decrypt the payload to the temp stream once, open the inner ZIP, locate only the requested entry, copy it through a HashingStream and run CheckEntry on it; leave ReadEntries for the small-packet case and document a size limit on it.

findings.issue: There is no known-answer vector for Argon2id. Every Argon2 test compares the implementation with itself, so a Konscious version change or a parameter-unit mistake (MemorySize is in KiB blocks) would not be caught, and the Android side must derive the same key from the same recovery code/password for the recovery sheet to work across devices.
findings.fix: Add one test pinning an RFC 9106 / published Argon2id vector (fixed password, salt, m, t, p → expected output hex) through Argon2Kdf.DeriveKey, and mirror the same vector in the Android test suite when B7 lands.

missing_spec_items: ARCHITECTURE §4 + AGREEMENT item 17 — the administrator's recovery copy (AdminWrap) for containers is not expressible: `.wakeel-backup` (password mode) and `.wakeel-msg`/`.wakeel-transfer`/`.wakeel-inventory` (sealedFor mode) carry no copy of the content key sealed to the organisation X25519 key, so the administrator cannot open a backup or a correspondence as the agreement requires. The installation key file's AdminWrap covers only the DbKey, not container payloads. Must be added before the signed manifest format ships (see finding on ContainerManifest.cs).

ARCHITECTURE §7 — the phone side of pairing has no way to build the org→pc→phone chain: PairingAcceptBody does not include the PC certificate and the QR payload carries no PC Ed25519 key, so neither PairingAccept.VerifySignature nor CertificateChain.Verify(phoneCert, ..., issuerCertificate) can be called on the phone with material it actually receives.

Spec item 5 / test list 'certificate chain … expired' — DeviceCertificateBody has no notAfter field (the spec fixed the field list), so 'expired' is only approximated by rejecting issuance more than one day in the future plus an optional caller-supplied maxAge window. Builder flagged this; it needs an owner decision before the first `.wakeel-setup` ships, because adding notAfter later breaks the signed body.

Spec item 2 — the printed grouping is 4-4-4-4-5 (XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXC), not the '5 groups of 4' the spec asks for; 21 characters cannot fit 20 slots, so the spec text itself is inconsistent and the owner must choose (4-4-4-4-4 plus a separated check character, or the current form).

Spec item 8 — PairingQrPayload carries an extra `issuedAt` beyond the five listed fields (needed so the phone can evaluate the ten-minute window from the image alone). Harmless but it is a deviation from the field list, and the QR payload is consumed by the Android app, so B7 must be told.
notes:
Commands run exactly as instructed, from D:\AI\Administration2: `dotnet build src/Wakeel.Crypto && dotnet test tests/Wakeel.Crypto.Tests`. Build succeeded with 0 warnings / 0 errors (TreatWarningsAsErrors=true from Directory.Build.props applies), tests: Failed 0, Passed 136, Skipped 0, Total 136, 6 s. I modified no file in the repository; two suspected defects were confirmed with a throwaway console probe built in the session scratchpad that references the compiled Wakeel.Crypto.dll (probe output quoted in the findings for the FormatException, the null Producer.Body, and the path-prefix escape).

Overall quality is high. Every numbered spec item is implemented; no package was added; Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props and Wakeel.slnx are untouched; no Windows-only API and no reference to any other Wakeel project; no Arabic in src (only §, × and → inside XML docs) — Arabic appears in tests only as payload data, which is the right way to prove UTF-8 handling. Primitive choices are sound: AES-256-GCM with a fresh random 12-byte nonce and an authenticated version byte, HKDF-SHA256 labels on every derived key, X25519 sealed boxes whose salt binds both public keys (NSec returns null for low-order points and that case is handled), Ed25519 over canonical JSON, Argon2id at 64 MB/3/2 with a floor of exactly 32 MB, FixedTimeEquals on the pairing token proof, TimeProvider everywhere time matters (no DateTime.Now anywhere in the project).

Test quality: the suite asserts real behaviour, not tautologies — wrong key, wrong associated data, wrong version byte, flipped bit, truncation, streaming at 0/1/4096/300000 bytes, both AutoTune branches driven by a stepping clock, manifest/payload/signature tampering separately plus a re-signed tampered payload (which correctly still fails at the entry hash), revoked/forged/future-dated/too-old certificates, a 3 MB streamed backup, and the full pairing exchange. Two blind spots stand out and both correspond to findings: nothing tests a container opened without an organisation key (the high finding), and nothing tests malformed manifest JSON (the FormatException/NRE finding).

API shape for downstream packages is usable as described in ARCHITECTURE.md, with the documented caveats: ContainerKeySource/ContainerWriteRequest/ContainerOpenOptions are clean seams for B1 (setup), B6 (sync/backup) and B7 (phone); KeyWraps + InstallationKeyFile match §3's three-wrap model plus AdminWrap; CertificateChain.TryVerify gives the UI a code without exception handling. The two shape changes that must land before other packages build on them, because they change signed/serialised formats, are the container AdminSealedKey and the PC certificate inside PairingAcceptBody.

Verdict is 'fix' solely because of the one high and six medium findings; none of them requires rewriting the design, and the low findings can be batched with them.
